text:
The number one question on every CEO's mind is "where should we start". 

Answered below.

Five bangers from OpenAI's Karan Singhal:

1. Raising the floor and the ceiling of human health:

"There's more than 300 million people weekly using ChatGPT for health and wellness types of questions, and we take that as an incredibly important responsibility to get that right."

"We're really invested in making sure basically two things. One is that we can raise the floor of human health and give people access to trustworthy, abundant, reliable health intelligence for free or nearly free, and really raise the ceiling as well and make things possible that weren't possible before."

2. Five physicians, eight answers:

"It turns out if you ask five physicians any question, you'll get, like, eight different answers. One of the first things that we did when we first started focusing on health at OpenAI was really build this kind of global physician network of hundreds of experts."

"[The goal was] to kind of aggregate the wisdom of experts so that we weren't relying, especially in areas where there could be disagreement, on one or two or three physicians to kind of adjudicate."

3. Why health runs on a general model rather than a specialized model:

"What we're talking about here is actually specialized training in a general model, which is, I think, actually the best of both worlds."

"If you forked and said, 'Hey, we're gonna train a smaller specialized model that is just for healthcare'... what you'd find is that model would fall behind the frontier relatively quickly, because the pace of the frontier and the general model improvements is so fast."

4. Compressing medicine's 5 to 17-year lag:

"How long does it take for clinical guidelines to penetrate the practice of everyday doctors across the world? People have found that this takes, depending on the study, 5 to 17 years... You don't wanna be practicing medicine 5 to 17 years behind."

"One of the things that we think about is how do you compress that kind of period of practicing down to weeks or days or even hours."

5. Healthcare's legacy software is ripe for agents:

"Healthcare is also one of those industries where you shouldn't expect everything to have an MCP connector tomorrow. It is a place where there's legacy software... This is absolutely ripe for agents and computer use."

 "This is a place where a lot of the barriers that have traditionally existed between patients and getting the care they need and clinicians and delivering the care they need and healthcare data in general... I think a lot of those will dissolve."

@thekaransinghal

text:
AI is on track to become a superhuman hardware designer, but design is only the beginning. The interface between bits and atoms is lossy, and turning designs into real hardware gets harder at every level:

1. Sourcing off-the-shelf parts that work together (a 2006 Falcon 1 engine test was delayed by one capacitor, in stock 6,000 miles away)

2. Custom parts, where a master machinist translates CAD into machine instructions

3. Assemblies, where every part can meet its drawing and still not fit

4. Outside vendors (even SpaceX has 591 employees with supply chain titles)

5. Doing all of it at a scale of 1,000,000

"Superhuman AI might be great at pure design, meaning at defining the platonically ideal part for a particular job, but struggle with 'design for manufacturing,' or finding a point design that meets the requirements while remaining easy to build/procure and inexpensive."

Full piece from a16z's Christian Keil on what it takes to turn AI-designed hardware into the real thing: https://www.a16z.news/p/superhuman-hardware-design-is-the

Karan Singhal of @OpenAI on the collapsing cost of intelligence, as seen on their health benchmark:

"GPT-6 Luna is our current cheapest frontier model on the API... It performed better than 5.6 Sol, which was literally our best model a month ago. And it performs better despite being 34x cheaper."

Most tiers of model intelligence became more than 100x cheaper within roughly a year

One tier went from ~$32 to ~$0.02 per million tokens in two years

text:
For AI to become a superhuman hardware engineer, it has to learn from the physical world, and real-world data is hard to get:

- It's non-uniform and constantly changing
- It's sparse: you can't measure everything all the time
- It's expensive to collect
- Physical processes take time, and can only be sped up so far
- Some of it is qualitative: do users actually like the product?

"Data limitations like these are massive drivers in the spikiness of AI capability development today. The more quantifiable and machine-readable the results of a test, the faster the models can climb the hill."

Full piece from a16z's Christian Keil on why the physical world is so hard for AI to learn from: https://www.a16z.news/p/superhuman-hardware-design-is-the

"It took me three months to design it, but it's nine months until I can actually start to use it."

Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger on the manufacturing bottleneck between designing hardware with AI and actually getting it built:

"Let's say we're off to do a great new chip together, the one that's gonna leap ahead because we have understanding of the AI workloads... And let's say we turn our AI tools loose. Within three months we have an awesome design."

"[But] we still have like a couple of really major bottlenecks today. One is we still have nine months of silicon processing time... So I can design the thing in three months, but I can't actually get it into real silicon at scale for nine months."

"We have to really see that bottleneck improve if we're gonna have this innovation."

"If it takes me a year and a half until I actually get scale and software on it, my understanding of the AI workloads is no longer applicable to the chip that I designed."

"All of those aspects somewhat obviate the fact that AI has made the design piece easy. All of those manufacturing scale issues to me become a huge bottleneck."

@PGelsinger @appenz @RaghuRaghuram

a16z's Christian Keil makes the case for why manufacturing, testing and iteration are the next frontier for AI in hardware: https://www.a16z.news/p/superhuman-hardware-design-is-the

AI models are getting close to designing hardware better than humans, and that shifts where the hard problems are:

- Better simulation, so physical builds become confirmation instead of experiments
- Demand shifts toward parts, machining and raw materials
- AI labs need to capture the "process knowledge" that lives in machinists and fabs

The one step even superhuman AI will struggle to speed up:

"A superhuman hardware engineer could design one million new iterations of the Apple Watch and get them manufactured for cheap, but then how can it know what customers actually want?"

But once AI crosses over, "the impact should prove immense: humanity will be able to directly use digital AI tools to bring about real, physical, material abundance."

Full piece from a16z's Christian Keil on what hardware engineering looks like once AI masters design: https://www.a16z.news/p/superhuman-hardware-design-is-the

Ekin Dogus Cubuk of @periodiclabs on why AI has to learn from the physical world, and building their own lab to close that loop:

"One of the more fundamental ways of making things around us is powder synthesis... You can actually, using that method, discover new superconductors, magnets, all kinds of materials that are very important for technologies around us."

"But at the core of it is just quantum mechanics. And we feel like teaching these LLMs quantum mechanics will be the next frontier for LLMs."

"Science is by its nature iterative, right? Like even the smartest humans tried many times before they discovered the things they discovered. LLMs can be very smart, but if they're not iterating on science, they won't discover science."

"The important thing to teach these LLMs is the method of scientific inquiry. So you do simulations, you do theoretical calculations, you do experiments, you get results, and the results are probably incorrect or not what you wanted at first, but you iterate on it."

"You have to do it with the real physics, not just the simulation."

@ekindogus @AnjneyMidha

a16z's Christian Keil makes the case for why building, testing, and iterating in the physical world is the bottleneck for AI in hardware: https://www.a16z.news/p/superhuman-hardware-design-is-the

Eugenia Kuyda, founder of @wabi, on why chatbots are the MS-DOS era of AI, and why a new interface is necessary to make AI's full potential obvious to everyone:

"It always struck me as strange that people were using products like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, but mostly for very simple use cases: for search, or to help them write something, help with homework."

"No one was really mentioning any of these exciting capabilities that we just kept seeing the models get, and so we felt like there must be an interface problem."

"There should be something simple for everyone, me included, to actually discover these amazing use cases that all these models already have."

"We got obsessed with this metaphor that the current chatbots are really the Microsoft DOS era for AI interfaces. And that there will be some sort of a Windows/MacOS moment."

"There is so much traction with chatbots... In order to unlock something else, you need a more exciting interface."

@ekuyda
